code_smells.summary: Test data is made up and silly (foo, bar, 123) instead of realistic.
code_smells.problem: Test data is made up and silly (foo, bar, 123) instead of realistic. Tests then miss real-world cases and are hard to read.
code_smells.bad_code: user = User('foo', 'bar@baz', 1)
code_smells.good_code: user = User('Asha Rao', 'asha.rao@example.com', age=34)
fix: Use data that looks like production.
Name things as in the real world.

quiz.question: Why use realistic test data?
choices: It reveals real-world problems and is easier to read
quiz.explanation: Good examples tell a story.

code_smells.title: Return False
code_smells.summary: A function returns True or False through nested checks instead of one clear boolean expression describing the rule.
code_smells.problem: A function returns True or False through nested checks instead of one clear boolean expression describing the rule.
code_smells.bad_code:
def can_vote(p):
    if p.age < 18: return False
    if not p.citizen: return False
    return True
code_smells.good_code:
def can_vote(p):
    return p.age >= 18 and p.citizen
fix: Write the rule as one expression.
Name the function after the question.

quiz.question: How can `if a: return False; if b: return False; return True` be shortened?
choices: return not a and not b
quiz.explanation: One clear formula shows the rule.

code_smells.title: Stairs Code
code_smells.summary: Several nested ifs build up a boolean result step by step, creating a staircase of code.
code_smells.problem: Several nested ifs build up a boolean result step by step, creating a staircase of code.
code_smells.good_code: return a and b
fix: Extract complex pieces into named functions.

quiz.question: Which is clearer?
quiz.explanation: Flat boolean logic is easier to verify.

code_smells.title: Sequential IDs
code_smells.summary: Records use numbers that count up (1, 2, 3...) as public ids.
code_smells.problem: Records use numbers that count up (1, 2, 3...) as public ids. Attackers can guess other ids and visitors can see how many you have.
code_smells.good_code: /invoices/7f3a9c1e-...   # UUID
fix: Use random, non-guessable ids (UUIDs) in public URLs.

quiz.question: Why avoid sequential ids in public URLs?
choices: They are easy to guess and reveal information
quiz.explanation: Random ids make enumeration attacks harder.

code_smells.title: String Validations
code_smells.summary: Input is checked with string operations (length, regex) in many places.
code_smells.problem: Input is checked with string operations (length, regex) in many places. The rules belong in a class that represents the concept.
code_smells.bad_code: if '@' in email and len(email) < 255: ...   # repeated everywhere
code_smells.good_code: email = Email(text)   # validates once in the constructor
fix: Create a class for the concept (Email, Phone).
Pass the object, not the raw string.

quiz.question: Where should email validation live?
choices: In every function that uses an email
quiz.explanation: Validate once; use valid objects everywhere.

code_smells.title: Primitive Obsession
code_smells.summary: Simple types like str, int and float are used for rich concepts (email, money, age).
code_smells.problem: Simple types like str, int and float are used for rich concepts (email, money, age). Their rules get repeated and invalid values slip through.
why_bad: Easy to mix up arguments of the same type.
code_smells.bad_code:
def send(email: str, amount: float): ...
send('oops', -5)
code_smells.good_code: def send(email: Email, amount: Money): ...

quiz.question: What does a small value object like Email give you?
choices: A guarantee that every Email is valid
quiz.explanation: Types carry meaning and rules.

code_smells.title: Mixed 'What' and 'How'
code_smells.summary: A function mixes 'what' the code is for with 'how' it does it, so readers have to decode loops and details to learn the goal.
code_smells.problem: A function mixes 'what' the code is for with 'how' it does it, so readers have to decode loops and details to learn the goal.
code_smells.good_code: total = sum(item.price for item in items)
fix: Express the goal with a clear name.

quiz.question: What does declarative code focus on?
choices: What you want, not how to get it
quiz.explanation: Say what, hide how.

code_smells.title: Divergent Change
code_smells.summary: One class changes for many unrelated reasons (new tax rule, new report format, new database), a sign that it holds several responsibilities.
code_smells.problem: One class changes for many unrelated reasons (new tax rule, new report format, new database), a sign that it holds several responsibilities.
why_bad: Every change touches the same file.
code_smells.bad_code: class Invoice:   # edited for tax rules, PDF layout and DB changes
code_smells.good_code:
class Invoice: ...
class InvoicePdf: ...
class InvoiceRepository: ...
fix: List the reasons the class changes.
Split each reason into its own class.

quiz.question: A class changes whenever tax, layout or storage changes. What smell is it?
quiz.explanation: One class, one reason to change.

code_smells.title: 'IS-A' Relationship
code_smells.summary: Inheritance is used because 'a Square is a Rectangle' in maths, but in code the child cannot honour the parent's rules.
code_smells.problem: Inheritance is used because 'a Square is a Rectangle' in maths, but in code the child cannot honour the parent's rules.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Square(Rectangle):
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = self.h = w   # breaks Rectangle
code_smells.good_code:
class Shape:
    def area(self): ...
class Square(Shape): ...
class Rectangle(Shape): ...
fix: Check that the child can replace the parent everywhere.
Think in terms of behavior, not categories.

quiz.question: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle say?
choices: A child must be usable wherever its parent is
quiz.explanation: Model behavior, not word-based 'is-a'.

code_smells.title: Fake Null Object
code_smells.summary: A special NullObject class is created even though a real object with empty values could play the same role.
code_smells.problem: A special NullObject class is created even though a real object with empty values could play the same role.
code_smells.bad_code: class NullCustomer(Customer): ...
code_smells.good_code: unknown = Customer(name='Unknown')
fix: Check whether a real object with default values works.

quiz.question: When do you not need a NullObject class?
choices: When a real object with default values works
quiz.explanation: Do not abuse even good patterns.

code_smells.title: Mutable Constants
code_smells.summary: A 'constant' such as a list or dict can be modified by anyone.
code_smells.problem: A 'constant' such as a list or dict can be modified by anyone. The constant changes during the run and breaks other code.
code_smells.bad_code:
COLORS = ['red', 'green']
COLORS.append('pink')   # everyone sees it
code_smells.good_code: COLORS = ('red', 'green')   # immutable tuple

quiz.question: Which is a safer constant in Python?
quiz.explanation: Immutable values cannot be changed by accident.

code_smells.title: Non English Coding
code_smells.summary: Names are written in a mix of languages (English keywords with local-language words).
code_smells.problem: Names are written in a mix of languages (English keywords with local-language words). It confuses readers and tools.
code_smells.bad_code: def calcular_total(precio): ...   # mixed with English keywords
code_smells.good_code: def calculate_total(price): ...
fix: Write comments in a shared language.

quiz.question: Why write identifiers in English?
choices: Programming languages and libraries already use it, so code stays consistent
quiz.explanation: A single language keeps code readable worldwide.

code_smells.title: Structural Optimizations
code_smells.summary: Code is made complicated 'for speed' without a real benchmark, hurting readability for guesses about performance.
code_smells.problem: Code is made complicated 'for speed' without a real benchmark, hurting readability for guesses about performance.
code_smells.bad_code: # manual loop unrolling for a function that runs once
code_smells.good_code: def total(items): return sum(i.price for i in items)

quiz.question: When should you optimise structure for performance?
choices: After a real benchmark shows a problem
quiz.explanation: Measure before you optimise.

code_smells.title: AddressImpl
code_smells.summary: Classes are named with suffixes like Impl (AddressImpl) that only describe how they are built, not what they are.
code_smells.problem: Classes are named with suffixes like Impl (AddressImpl) that only describe how they are built, not what they are.
why_bad: Names do not describe the concept.
Hard to find the real name.
code_smells.bad_code: class AddressImpl(Address): ...
code_smells.good_code: class PostalAddress: ...

quiz.question: Which name is best?
quiz.explanation: Names should come from the domain.

code_smells.title: Zero Argument Constructor
code_smells.summary: An object is created with no arguments and then filled in by setters.
code_smells.problem: An object is created with no arguments and then filled in by setters. Until then it is incomplete.
code_smells.bad_code:
u = User()
u.name = 'Asha'
code_smells.good_code: u = User(name='Asha', email='a@x.com')
fix: Pass all essential values to the constructor.
Make the object ready from the start.

quiz.question: Why prefer one full constructor?
choices: The object is valid from the moment it exists
quiz.explanation: Complete at creation, valid forever.

code_smells.title: Exception Try Too Broad
code_smells.summary: A try block wraps many lines or catches Exception.
code_smells.problem: A try block wraps many lines or catches Exception. Errors from unrelated code are caught and mistaken for the expected one.
fix: Wrap only the line that can fail.

quiz.question: How narrow should a try/except be?
choices: As narrow as possible: one risky call, one specific exception
quiz.explanation: Specific handlers keep real bugs visible.

code_smells.title: Hardcoded IF Conditions
code_smells.summary: Conditions contain fixed values (if status == 'gold') scattered through the code.
code_smells.problem: Conditions contain fixed values (if status == 'gold') scattered through the code. Adding a new value means editing every place.
code_smells.bad_code:
if tier == 'gold': discount = 0.2
elif tier == 'silver': discount = 0.1
code_smells.good_code:
DISCOUNTS = {'gold': 0.2, 'silver': 0.1}
discount = DISCOUNTS[tier]
fix: Replace repeated ifs with a lookup table or objects.
Keep the values in one place.
Add a new tier by adding data.

quiz.question: How do you avoid growing an if/elif chain of fixed values?
choices: Use a lookup table or polymorphism
quiz.explanation: Data-driven code grows without edits.

code_smells.title: Specialized Business Collections
code_smells.summary: A special class wraps a standard collection (OrderList, UserSet) without adding any behavior.
code_smells.problem: A special class wraps a standard collection (OrderList, UserSet) without adding any behavior.
code_smells.bad_code: class UserList(list): pass
code_smells.good_code: users = []   # a plain list is enough
fix: Check if the wrapper adds behavior.
If not, use the standard collection.
Add a class when real behavior appears.

quiz.question: When is a custom collection class worth it?
choices: When it adds real behavior or rules
quiz.explanation: Do not wrap for wrapping's sake.

code_smells.title: Interfaces With just One Realization
code_smells.summary: An interface is defined with exactly one implementation, 'in case there will be more'.
code_smells.problem: An interface is defined with exactly one implementation, 'in case there will be more'.
code_smells.bad_code:
class IMailer: ...
class Mailer(IMailer): ...   # the only one
code_smells.good_code: class Mailer: ...
fix: Add it when a second implementation appears.

quiz.question: When should you introduce an interface?
choices: When there are at least two real implementations
quiz.explanation: Abstract after you have examples.

code_smells.title: Classes With just One Subclass
code_smells.summary: A base class is created with a single child, 'for future variants'.
code_smells.problem: A base class is created with a single child, 'for future variants'.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Vehicle: ...
class Car(Vehicle): ...   # only subclass
code_smells.good_code: class Car: ...

quiz.question: A class has just one subclass. What should you consider?
choices: Merging them until a second subclass appears
quiz.explanation: Generalise when you have more than one case.

code_smells.title: Inheritance Tree Too Deep
code_smells.summary: A class sits at the bottom of a long chain of parents.
code_smells.problem: A class sits at the bottom of a long chain of parents. To understand one method you must read many files, and a change in a parent can break many children.
code_smells.bad_code:
class A: ...
class B(A): ...
class C(B): ...
class D(C): ...
class E(D): ...
fix: Keep inheritance for true is-a cases.

quiz.question: What should you use instead of very deep inheritance?
quiz.explanation: Small objects combined are more flexible.

code_smells.title: Packages Dependency
code_smells.summary: A project pulls in a big package for a tiny task, or trusts many dependencies without checking.
code_smells.problem: A project pulls in a big package for a tiny task, or trusts many dependencies without checking. Each one adds risk and maintenance.
code_smells.bad_code: import left_pad   # one line of code
code_smells.good_code: def left_pad(s, n): return s.rjust(n)
fix: Use well-known, maintained libraries for hard problems.

quiz.question: When is it better to write the code yourself?
quiz.explanation: Every dependency has a cost.

code_smells.title: Business Code in the User Interface
code_smells.summary: Business rules (validation, pricing) live in the user interface.
code_smells.problem: Business rules (validation, pricing) live in the user interface. Other clients, such as an API or mobile app, must copy them, and users can bypass them.
code_smells.bad_code:
// only the web form checks the age
if (age < 18) showError();
code_smells.good_code:
# back-end
if age < 18: raise ValueError('must be 18+')

quiz.question: Where should important validation happen?
choices: In the back-end (the UI may also check for convenience)
quiz.explanation: The server must never trust the client.

code_smells.title: Short Circuit Evaluation
code_smells.summary: Expensive or side-effect checks are done even when the first check already decides the result.
code_smells.problem: Expensive or side-effect checks are done even when the first check already decides the result. Short-circuiting avoids needless work.
code_smells.bad_code: ok = a() & b()   # & always evaluates both
code_smells.good_code: ok = a() and b()   # b() runs only if a() is true
fix: Put cheap or likely-failing checks first.

quiz.question: What does `a() and b()` do if a() is False?
quiz.explanation: Short-circuit skips unnecessary work.

code_smells.title: IEngine , AVehicle, ImplCar
code_smells.summary: Classes are prefixed or suffixed with I, A, Impl or Base (IEngine, AVehicle, ImplCar).
code_smells.problem: Classes are prefixed or suffixed with I, A, Impl or Base (IEngine, AVehicle, ImplCar). The prefix describes the mechanics, not the concept.
code_smells.bad_code:
class IEngine: ...
class ImplEngine(IEngine): ...
code_smells.good_code:
class Engine: ...
class ElectricEngine(Engine): ...
fix: Name classes after what they are.

quiz.question: Which name is better?
quiz.explanation: Concept names, not technical decorations.

code_smells.title: Queries in Constructors
code_smells.summary: A constructor runs database queries or network calls.
code_smells.problem: A constructor runs database queries or network calls. Creating an object becomes slow, can fail, and is hard to test.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Report:
    def __init__(self, id): self.rows = db.query(id)

quiz.question: What should a constructor do?
choices: Set up the object from the values given
quiz.explanation: Constructors should construct, nothing more.

code_smells.title: Data Clumps
code_smells.summary: The same few values (start_date, end_date) are passed around together in many signatures.
code_smells.problem: The same few values (start_date, end_date) are passed around together in many signatures. They belong in a small object.
code_smells.bad_code:
def book(start, end): ...
def cancel(start, end): ...

quiz.question: start and end dates always appear together. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: A named concept removes repetition.

code_smells.title: Fungible Objects
code_smells.summary: Objects that should be interchangeable (every 1-rupee coin) are modelled with unique identity, or unique things are modelled as interchangeable.
code_smells.problem: Objects that should be interchangeable (every 1-rupee coin) are modelled with unique identity, or unique things are modelled as interchangeable.
code_smells.bad_code: Coin(id=1) != Coin(id=2)   # but all 1-rupee coins are equal
code_smells.good_code: Coin(value=1) == Coin(value=1)
fix: Ask: in reality, can this be swapped for another?
Use value equality for fungible things.

quiz.question: Which object is fungible in the real world?
quiz.explanation: Model equality the way the real thing behaves.

code_smells.title: Short Circuit Hack
code_smells.summary: A function with side effects is called inside a boolean expression (`ok and save()`), so whether it runs depends on a hidden short-circuit rule.
code_smells.problem: A function with side effects is called inside a boolean expression (`ok and save()`), so whether it runs depends on a hidden short-circuit rule.
code_smells.bad_code: user and log_in(user)
code_smells.good_code:
if user:
    log_in(user)
fix: Do not rely on short-circuiting for side effects.

quiz.question: Why is `user and log_in(user)` unclear?
choices: It hides a side effect inside an expression
quiz.explanation: Make side effects obvious with if.

code_smells.title: Getter Comments
code_smells.summary: Getters are given comments like '# returns the name'.
code_smells.problem: Getters are given comments like '# returns the name'. The comment repeats the obvious, and the getter itself is a smell.
code_smells.bad_code:
# Returns the name
def get_name(self): return self._name
code_smells.good_code: # no comment, no getter; expose behavior instead

quiz.question: Should you comment `get_name()`?
quiz.explanation: Do not comment the obvious.

code_smells.title: Too Many Methods
code_smells.summary: A class has dozens of public methods for unrelated tasks.
code_smells.problem: A class has dozens of public methods for unrelated tasks. It is hard to learn and change.
code_smells.bad_code: class Service:   # 60 methods
code_smells.good_code:
class Orders: ...
class Customers: ...
class Invoices: ...
fix: Extract each group into a class.

quiz.question: A class has 60 methods. What should you do?
choices: Split it into several focused classes
quiz.explanation: Smaller classes are easier to understand.

code_smells.title: ToDos
code_smells.summary: TODO comments are left in the code and never done.
code_smells.problem: TODO comments are left in the code and never done. They become permanent notes about problems nobody fixes.
code_smells.bad_code:
# TODO: handle negative numbers
def sqrt(x): ...
code_smells.good_code:
def sqrt(x):
    if x < 0: raise ValueError('x must be >= 0')
fix: Or move it to an issue tracker.

quiz.question: What is the best place for work you can't do now?
quiz.explanation: Tracked work gets done.

code_smells.title: Optional Chaining
code_smells.summary: Optional chaining (?.) is used everywhere to dodge nulls.
code_smells.problem: Optional chaining (?.) is used everywhere to dodge nulls. It hides the real problem: values that should never be null.
code_smells.bad_code: user?.address?.city?.toUpperCase()
code_smells.good_code: user.shippingCity()   // never null

quiz.question: What does heavy use of `?.` suggest?
choices: Too many nullable values in the design
quiz.explanation: Fix the cause rather than chaining around it.

code_smells.title: Equal Comparison
code_smells.summary: Code fetches two values and compares them outside (`a.id == b.id`) instead of asking `a.equals(b)`.
code_smells.problem: Code fetches two values and compares them outside (`a.id == b.id`) instead of asking `a.equals(b)`.
code_smells.bad_code: if a.id == b.id and a.type == b.type: ...
code_smells.good_code: if a == b: ...   # __eq__ defined once
fix: Do not export fields to compare.

quiz.question: Where should comparison logic live?
quiz.explanation: Let the object decide if it is equal.

code_smells.title: Commented Code
code_smells.summary: Old code is commented out 'just in case'.
code_smells.problem: Old code is commented out 'just in case'. It adds noise, never runs and is not tested.
code_smells.bad_code:
# total = price * 0.9
total = price * 0.85
code_smells.good_code: total = price * 0.85
fix: Use git to see old versions.

quiz.question: What should you do with commented-out code?
quiz.explanation: Version control is the memory.

code_smells.title: Logical Comment
code_smells.summary: Code is skipped by changing its logic (`if False:` or `and 0`) instead of removing it.
code_smells.problem: Code is skipped by changing its logic (`if False:` or `and 0`) instead of removing it. The hack hides what is happening.
code_smells.bad_code: if False and user.admin: ...
code_smells.good_code: # remove it, or use a named flag/feature toggle
fix: Delete the code or use an explicit toggle.

quiz.question: What is wrong with `if False: ...`?
choices: The skipped code is hidden dead code
quiz.explanation: Remove or make the toggle explicit.

code_smells.title: Too Long Names
code_smells.summary: Names are so long they read like sentences (get_the_total_price_of_all_items_in_cart_with_tax).
code_smells.problem: Names are so long they read like sentences (get_the_total_price_of_all_items_in_cart_with_tax). Too long is as hard to read as too short.
why_bad: Often hides a function doing too much.
code_smells.bad_code: def calculate_the_total_amount_with_tax_and_shipping_for_cart(): ...
code_smells.good_code: def cart_total(): ...
fix: If a name needs many 'and's, split the function.

quiz.question: Which name is best?
quiz.explanation: Aim for a name just long enough to be clear.

code_smells.title: Too Many Variables
code_smells.summary: A function declares many local variables early and uses them far away.
code_smells.problem: A function declares many local variables early and uses them far away. Readers must keep track of all of them.
code_smells.bad_code: a=1; b=2; c=3; d=4; ...   # used 40 lines later
code_smells.good_code: # declare each variable next to where it is used

quiz.question: Where should a variable be declared?
choices: As close as possible to where it is used
At the top of the file
quiz.explanation: Short scopes are easier to follow.

code_smells.title: Multiple Promises
code_smells.summary: Async calls are awaited one after another even though they are independent, wasting time.
code_smells.problem: Async calls are awaited one after another even though they are independent, wasting time.
code_smells.bad_code:
a = await fetch_a()
b = await fetch_b()   # waits for a first
code_smells.good_code: a, b = await asyncio.gather(fetch_a(), fetch_b())
fix: Only await in sequence when order matters.

quiz.question: How do you run two independent awaits at the same time?
quiz.explanation: Run independent work in parallel.

code_smells.title: Implicit Else
code_smells.summary: An if has no else, so the reader cannot tell if 'nothing happens' is intended or forgotten.
code_smells.problem: An if has no else, so the reader cannot tell if 'nothing happens' is intended or forgotten.
code_smells.bad_code:
if user.is_admin:
    grant()
fix: Say what happens in every case.

quiz.question: Why write an explicit else?
choices: It shows every case was considered
quiz.explanation: Explicit is better than implicit.

code_smells.title: Balance at 0
code_smells.summary: A missing balance, an error and a real balance of zero are all shown as 0.
code_smells.problem: A missing balance, an error and a real balance of zero are all shown as 0. Users cannot tell them apart.
code_smells.bad_code: balance = fetch() or 0   # error looks like zero
code_smells.good_code: balance = fetch()   # raises BalanceUnavailable on failure
fix: Treat zero and errors as different.
Raise or return a clear error value.
Show a message in the UI.

quiz.question: Why is showing 0 for an error bad?
choices: Users cannot tell zero from a failure
quiz.explanation: Zero is a value, not an error.

code_smells.title: Variables not Variable
code_smells.summary: A variable that never changes is declared as if it could, so readers must check every line to be sure it stays the same.
code_smells.problem: A variable that never changes is declared as if it could, so readers must check every line to be sure it stays the same.
why_bad: Readers cannot tell what may change.
code_smells.bad_code: rate = 0.18   # never changed, but looks changeable
code_smells.good_code: GST_RATE = 0.18   # named constant: obviously fixed
fix: Find values that are assigned once.
Keep only truly changing values as variables.

quiz.question: How should a value that never changes be declared?
quiz.explanation: Constants tell the reader the value is stable.

code_smells.title: Mixed Case
code_smells.summary: Names mix styles (camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase) in the same code.
code_smells.problem: Names mix styles (camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase) in the same code. Readers waste time and tools get confused.
code_smells.bad_code:
def getUser_name(): ...
user_Id = 1
code_smells.good_code:
def get_user_name(): ...
user_id = 1

quiz.question: Which is the PEP 8 style for function names?
quiz.explanation: One convention makes code predictable.

code_smells.title: Invalid Id = 9999
code_smells.summary: A magic id like 9999 or -1 means 'invalid' or 'no user', but it can also be a real id later.
code_smells.problem: A magic id like 9999 or -1 means 'invalid' or 'no user', but it can also be a real id later. Callers must remember the special value.
why_bad: The special id may become real.
Every caller must check for it.
It mixes real data with signals.
code_smells.bad_code: user_id = -1   # means 'guest'
code_smells.good_code: user = GuestUser()   # a Null Object with the same methods
fix: Model the special case with its own object.
Return that object instead of a code.

quiz.question: What is better than using -1 as a 'no user' id?
quiz.explanation: Special cases deserve their own objects.

code_smells.title: Abstract/Final/Undefined Classes
code_smells.summary: Classes are neither abstract nor final: any class can be subclassed, even when the author never meant it.
code_smells.problem: Classes are neither abstract nor final: any class can be subclassed, even when the author never meant it. Overrides and surprises follow.
why_bad: Hard to know what is safe to extend.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Order: ...        # someone subclasses it without any plan
class SpecialOrder(Order): ...

quiz.question: In a healthy hierarchy, concrete classes should be...
quiz.explanation: Be explicit about what can be extended.

code_smells.title: Too Many Parentheses
code_smells.summary: Expressions are wrapped in extra parentheses that are not needed.
code_smells.problem: Expressions are wrapped in extra parentheses that are not needed. They add visual noise and hide the real grouping.
code_smells.good_code:
x = (a + b) * c

code_smells.problem: JavaScript `var` declarations are 'hoisted' to the top of the function, so a variable can be used before it is assigned.
code_smells.bad_code:
console.log(x);   // undefined, not an error
var x = 5;
code_smells.good_code:
const x = 5;
console.log(x);
fix: Declare variables at the top of their scope.

quiz.question: What does `console.log(x); var x = 5;` print in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Hoisting moves declarations, not values.

code_smells.title: Duplicate Parameter Names
code_smells.summary: A function declares two parameters with the same name.
code_smells.problem: A function declares two parameters with the same name. In non-strict JavaScript the last one silently wins, so an argument is lost.
code_smells.bad_code: function add(a, a) { return a; }   // second a wins
code_smells.good_code:
'use strict';
function add(first, second) { return first + second; }
fix: Give every parameter a unique, role-based name.

quiz.question: What does strict mode do for duplicate parameter names?
quiz.explanation: Strict mode turns silent bugs into errors.

code_smells.title: Deserializing Object Vulnerability
code_smells.summary: An app loads objects from data sent by users (pickle, unsafe YAML).
code_smells.problem: An app loads objects from data sent by users (pickle, unsafe YAML). The data can contain code that runs on your server.
code_smells.bad_code:
import pickle
obj = pickle.loads(request.body)   # runs attacker's code
code_smells.good_code:
import json
obj = json.loads(request.body)   # data only
fix: Accept data formats that cannot run code (JSON).

quiz.question: Why is `pickle.loads(user_data)` dangerous?
choices: It can execute code embedded in the data
quiz.explanation: Only deserialize data, never code.

code_smells.title: Fat Interface
code_smells.summary: An interface has many methods, and classes must implement ones they do not need.
code_smells.problem: An interface has many methods, and classes must implement ones they do not need. Changes to it affect everyone.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Machine:
    def print(self): ...
    def scan(self): ...
    def fax(self): ...
code_smells.good_code:
class Printer: ...
class Scanner: ...
class FaxMachine: ...
fix: Let classes pick what they need.

quiz.question: Which principle says to split fat interfaces?
quiz.explanation: Clients should not depend on methods they do not use.

code_smells.title: Empty Implementation
code_smells.summary: A method is implemented as empty (`pass`) just to satisfy an interface.
code_smells.problem: A method is implemented as empty (`pass`) just to satisfy an interface. Calling it silently does nothing.
code_smells.bad_code: def save(self): pass   # does nothing
code_smells.good_code:
def save(self):
    raise NotImplementedError('save is not supported yet')

quiz.question: What should an unimplemented method do?
quiz.explanation: Fail loudly so the gap is noticed.

code_smells.title: Magic Concatenation
code_smells.summary: Concatenating values with + behaves differently by type: '1' + 1 is an error in Python but '11' in JavaScript, and 1 + 1 is 2.
code_smells.problem: Concatenating values with + behaves differently by type: '1' + 1 is an error in Python but '11' in JavaScript, and 1 + 1 is 2.
code_smells.bad_code: '5' + 3   // '53' in JavaScript

quiz.question: What does '5' + 3 give in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Be explicit about types.

code_smells.title: Looping from index 0
code_smells.summary: Loops count from 0 while people count from 1.
code_smells.problem: Loops count from 0 while people count from 1. Index arithmetic (i - 1, n + 1) creates off-by-one errors.
code_smells.bad_code:
for i in range(len(chapters)):
    print(i, chapters[i])   # first chapter shows 0
code_smells.good_code:
for number, chapter in enumerate(chapters, start=1):
    print(number, chapter)
fix: Loop over items instead of indexes.

quiz.question: How do you number items starting at 1 in Python?
quiz.explanation: Match how people count.

code_smells.title: Return Tuple
code_smells.summary: A function returns several values in a tuple, so callers must remember the order.
code_smells.problem: A function returns several values in a tuple, so callers must remember the order. The result has no name or behavior.
why_bad: Order is easy to mix up.
code_smells.bad_code:
def stats(xs): return min(xs), max(xs), sum(xs)/len(xs)
low, avg, high = stats(xs)   # wrong order!
fix: Create a small object for the result.

quiz.question: What is safer than returning a tuple of three values?
quiz.explanation: Names beat positions.

code_smells.title: Missing Break in Switch
code_smells.summary: In languages with switch/case, forgetting `break` makes execution fall through into the next case.
code_smells.problem: In languages with switch/case, forgetting `break` makes execution fall through into the next case. Python has no switch, but the idea shows in match fall-through and repeated ifs.

quiz.question: What happens when `break` is missing in a switch case?
choices: Execution falls through to the next case
quiz.explanation: Fall-through is usually a mistake.

code_smells.title: Comma Operator
code_smells.summary: The comma operator runs several expressions in one statement (a(), b(), c()).
code_smells.problem: The comma operator runs several expressions in one statement (a(), b(), c()). Only the last value is kept, which confuses readers.
fix: Use the comma only in for-loops.

quiz.question: Why avoid the comma operator?
choices: It hides several steps inside one expression
quiz.explanation: One idea per statement.

code_smells.title: Racial Naming
code_smells.summary: Terms like whitelist, blacklist or master/slave carry negative meanings and exclude people.
code_smells.problem: Terms like whitelist, blacklist or master/slave carry negative meanings and exclude people. Clearer, neutral terms exist.
code_smells.bad_code:
blacklist = ['spam.com']
whitelist = ['mine.com']
code_smells.good_code:
denylist = ['spam.com']
allowlist = ['mine.com']

quiz.question: What is a neutral replacement for 'whitelist'?
quiz.explanation: Clearer names are also more inclusive.

code_smells.title: Deodorant Comments
code_smells.summary: Comments apologise for ugly code ('hack', 'sorry', 'don't ask').
code_smells.problem: Comments apologise for ugly code ('hack', 'sorry', 'don't ask'). The comment stays and the code is never fixed.
code_smells.bad_code:
# sorry, this is a mess
x = a if b else c if d else e
code_smells.good_code:
# rewrite the code and remove the comment
x = pick(a, b, c, d, e)

quiz.question: What should you do instead of adding an apology comment?
quiz.explanation: Fix the smell, do not label it.

code_smells.title: Pass by Reference
code_smells.summary: A function changes the list or object it receives.
code_smells.problem: A function changes the list or object it receives. The caller's data is modified without notice.
code_smells.bad_code:
def add_tax(items):
    for i in items: i.price *= 1.18
code_smells.good_code:
def with_tax(items):
    return [replace(i, price=i.price * 1.18) for i in items]

quiz.question: What is a safe way to change a list passed as an argument?
choices: Work on a copy and return it
quiz.explanation: Do not modify what you do not own.

code_smells.title: Mixed Priorities
code_smells.summary: Teams spend money on hardware to cover for poor software design and testing instead of making the software reliable.
code_smells.problem: Teams spend money on hardware to cover for poor software design and testing instead of making the software reliable.
code_smells.bad_code: # add more servers instead of fixing the slow query
code_smells.good_code: # profile, fix the query, and test failure cases

quiz.question: What is cheaper than buying more hardware to hide bugs?
choices: Designing and testing the software better
quiz.explanation: Software is cheaper to fix than hardware.

code_smells.title: Cowboy Coding
code_smells.summary: A developer works alone, ignores team rules and writes cryptic code that only they understand.
code_smells.problem: A developer works alone, ignores team rules and writes cryptic code that only they understand.
code_smells.bad_code: def f(a,b,c): return a*b+c-a%b   # cryptic
code_smells.good_code: def total_price(unit_price, quantity, shipping): ...

quiz.question: What is a sign of cowboy coding?
quiz.explanation: Code is a team asset.

code_smells.title: Multiple Classes per File
code_smells.summary: Several classes are placed in one file.
code_smells.problem: Several classes are placed in one file. Finding, testing and merging them becomes harder.
code_smells.bad_code: # models.py contains 25 unrelated classes
code_smells.good_code: # one concept per module: order.py, customer.py, invoice.py
fix: Move each class into its own file or module.

quiz.question: Why prefer one class per file (or small cohesive modules)?
choices: Easier navigation and fewer merge conflicts
quiz.explanation: Organise code so people can find it.

code_smells.title: Red Tape
code_smells.summary: Layers of forms, wrappers and approvals add work but no value.
code_smells.problem: Layers of forms, wrappers and approvals add work but no value. The domain is hidden behind bureaucracy.
why_bad: Hard to see the real model.
code_smells.bad_code: RequestBuilderFactoryManager().create().build().execute()
code_smells.good_code: order.ship()

quiz.question: What is 'red tape' in code?
choices: Needless layers that add complexity without value
quiz.explanation: Keep only the layers that earn their keep.

code_smells.title: Schrödinger Code
code_smells.summary: Code behaves differently depending on which thread runs first (a race condition).
code_smells.problem: Code behaves differently depending on which thread runs first (a race condition). The result is unpredictable, like Schrödinger's cat.
code_smells.bad_code:
counter = 0
def inc(): global counter; counter += 1   # two threads: lost updates
fix: Use locks, queues or atomic operations.

quiz.question: What causes a race condition?
choices: Unsynchronised access to shared data by several threads
quiz.explanation: Synchronise shared state.

code_smells.title: Redundant Data
code_smells.summary: The same fact is stored in two places (a total and the list it comes from).
code_smells.problem: The same fact is stored in two places (a total and the list it comes from). When one changes, they disagree.
code_smells.bad_code:
order.items = [...]
order.total = 250   # must be kept in sync by hand
code_smells.good_code: def total(self): return sum(i.price for i in self.items)

quiz.question: How do you avoid storing the same fact twice?
choices: Compute derived values from one source
quiz.explanation: Say it only once.

code_smells.title: Reusable Code
code_smells.summary: Similar code appears in several places.
code_smells.problem: Similar code appears in several places. The repetition hides an abstraction that has not been named yet.
code_smells.bad_code:
if kind == 'a': log('a'); save(a)
if kind == 'b': log('b'); save(b)
code_smells.good_code:
def record(x): log(x); save(x)
record(a); record(b)

quiz.question: What can repeated code reveal?
quiz.explanation: Duplication hints at a concept to extract.

code_smells.title: Collections Count
code_smells.summary: Names with 'count', 'size' or 'collection' don't say what is being counted or collected.
code_smells.problem: Names with 'count', 'size' or 'collection' don't say what is being counted or collected.
code_smells.bad_code: count = len(users)   # active? all? new?
code_smells.good_code: active_user_count = len(active_users)

quiz.question: Which name is clearest?
quiz.explanation: Narrow names remove ambiguity.

code_smells.title: Long Circuit
code_smells.summary: Boolean checks are ordered randomly, so slow checks (database call) run before cheap ones (is None).
code_smells.problem: Boolean checks are ordered randomly, so slow checks (database call) run before cheap ones (is None).
code_smells.bad_code: if db.has_access(user) and user is not None: ...
code_smells.good_code: if user is not None and db.has_access(user): ...

quiz.question: In `a and b`, which should go first?
choices: The cheaper and more selective check
quiz.explanation: Short-circuiting skips the rest.

code_smells.title: Console Side Effects
code_smells.summary: Functions print to the console directly.
code_smells.problem: Functions print to the console directly. They cannot be reused or tested without printing, and the output goes only one place.
code_smells.bad_code:
def report(rows):
    for r in rows: print(r)
code_smells.good_code:
def report(rows, out=sys.stdout):
    for r in rows: print(r, file=out)
fix: Or pass the output destination in.

quiz.question: How do you test a function that prints?
choices: Pass the output stream in, or return the text
quiz.explanation: Separate producing output from showing it.

code_smells.title: Unwrapped Lines
code_smells.summary: Lines are very long (more than 100 characters), so readers scroll sideways or the code is hard to read on small screens.
code_smells.problem: Lines are very long (more than 100 characters), so readers scroll sideways or the code is hard to read on small screens.
why_bad: Hard to review side by side.
code_smells.bad_code: result = service.get_customer(id).get_orders().filter(status='open').sort_by('date').first().total()
code_smells.good_code:
orders = service.open_orders(customer_id)
latest = orders.latest()
result = latest.total()

quiz.question: What line length does PEP 8 recommend?
quiz.explanation: Short lines are easier to read and compare.

code_smells.title: Attribute Definitions
code_smells.summary: A class is designed by listing its attributes first, instead of the behavior it must provide.
code_smells.problem: A class is designed by listing its attributes first, instead of the behavior it must provide. It becomes a data bag.
code_smells.bad_code:
class User:
    name; email; password_hash; created_at ...
fix: Start with what the object does.
Add attributes only to support behavior.

quiz.question: What should you design first?
quiz.explanation: Behavior first, data second.

code_smells.title: Entangled Code
code_smells.summary: Related lines are far apart in a function, with unrelated code in between.
code_smells.problem: Related lines are far apart in a function, with unrelated code in between. The reader has to jump back and forth.
code_smells.bad_code:
a = load_a()
b = load_b()
x = process(a)
y = process(b)
print(x, y)
code_smells.good_code:
a = load_a()
x = process(a)

b = load_b()
y = process(b)

quiz.question: What does entangled code need?
quiz.explanation: Keep what belongs together close.

code_smells.title: Big Pull Request
code_smells.summary: A pull request changes dozens of files and thousands of lines.
code_smells.problem: A pull request changes dozens of files and thousands of lines. Reviewers skim it, bugs slip in and merges conflict.
code_smells.bad_code: # PR: 3,200 lines, 70 files, 'misc improvements'
code_smells.good_code: # PR 1: rename. PR 2: new model. PR 3: use it. Each under ~300 lines.

quiz.question: What makes a good pull request?
choices: Small and focused on one change
quiz.explanation: Baby steps are easy to review.

code_smells.title: Dead Store
code_smells.summary: A variable is assigned a value that is overwritten before it is ever used.
code_smells.problem: A variable is assigned a value that is overwritten before it is ever used. The first assignment does nothing.
code_smells.bad_code:
x = expensive()
x = 5
fix: Keep only what has an effect.

quiz.question: What is a 'dead store'?
choices: A value that is assigned but never used
quiz.explanation: Remove code with no effect.

code_smells.title: Referential Transparency Violation
code_smells.summary: A function cannot be replaced by its result because it depends on hidden state (time, globals) or changes things.
code_smells.problem: A function cannot be replaced by its result because it depends on hidden state (time, globals) or changes things. Calls with the same input differ.
code_smells.bad_code: def price(x): return x * RATE   # RATE changes at runtime
code_smells.good_code: def price(x, rate): return x * rate

quiz.question: What is referential transparency?
choices: A call can be replaced by its result without changing the program
quiz.explanation: Same input, same output.

code_smells.title: Zombie Feature Flags
code_smells.summary: Old feature flags stay in the code long after the feature is released.
code_smells.problem: Old feature flags stay in the code long after the feature is released. Both code paths remain and nobody knows which is live.
code_smells.bad_code:
if flags.NEW_CHECKOUT:   # on in production since 2023
    new()
else:
    old()
code_smells.good_code: new()   # flag and old path removed
fix: Give every flag an owner and an end date.

quiz.question: What should happen to a feature flag after full rollout?
choices: Remove it and delete the old code
quiz.explanation: Flags are temporary.

code_smells.title: Concatenated Properties
code_smells.summary: Several independent things are glued into one string or property (full_name_and_title), so changing one part affects the rest.
code_smells.problem: Several independent things are glued into one string or property (full_name_and_title), so changing one part affects the rest.
code_smells.bad_code: user.name_and_email = 'Asha <a@x.com>'
code_smells.good_code:
user.name = 'Asha'
user.email = 'a@x.com'

quiz.question: Why avoid concatenating unrelated properties into one?
choices: They cannot be changed or validated independently
quiz.explanation: One attribute, one idea.

code_smells.title: Incomplete Error information
code_smells.summary: Error messages lack the facts needed to understand them: which file, which id, which value.
code_smells.problem: Error messages lack the facts needed to understand them: which file, which id, which value.
code_smells.bad_code: raise ValueError('not found')
code_smells.good_code: raise ValueError(f'user {user_id} not found in tenant {tenant}')

quiz.question: What information helps most in an error message?
choices: The value, the place and what was expected
quiz.explanation: Detailed errors speed debugging.

code_smells.title: exec() and eval()
code_smells.summary: Code runs strings as code with eval() or exec().
code_smells.problem: Code runs strings as code with eval() or exec(). Anyone who controls the string controls your program.
code_smells.bad_code: result = eval(user_input)   # '__import__("os").system("rm -rf /")'
code_smells.good_code:
import ast
result = ast.literal_eval(user_input)   # data only

quiz.question: What is a safe alternative to eval for parsing literal data?
quiz.explanation: Never run user-controlled strings as code.

code_smells.title: Expiration Date
code_smells.summary: An expiry date is stored as a plain date and compared everywhere, with each place defining 'expired' slightly differently.
code_smells.problem: An expiry date is stored as a plain date and compared everywhere, with each place defining 'expired' slightly differently.
code_smells.bad_code: if food.use_by < today: ...   # repeated in many places
code_smells.good_code:
class ExpirationDate:
    def is_expired_on(self, day): return self.day < day

quiz.question: Where should 'is expired' logic live?
quiz.explanation: Model the real concept.

code_smells.title: Javascript Replace
code_smells.summary: In JavaScript, `'a-b-c'.replace('-', '')` replaces only the first match, not all.
code_smells.problem: In JavaScript, `'a-b-c'.replace('-', '')` replaces only the first match, not all. The name suggests otherwise.
code_smells.bad_code: 'a-b-c'.replace('-', '')   // 'ab-c'
code_smells.good_code: 'a-b-c'.replaceAll('-', '')   // 'abc'
fix: Use replaceAll or a global regex.

quiz.question: What does `'a-b-c'.replace('-', '')` return in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Names can mislead; check the behavior.

code_smells.title: Unreliable Copy
code_smells.summary: A copy function is trusted to work but silently copies only part of the data (or only references), and nobody checks the result.
code_smells.problem: A copy function is trusted to work but silently copies only part of the data (or only references), and nobody checks the result.
code_smells.bad_code: b = a.copy()   # shallow: nested lists are shared
code_smells.good_code:
import copy
b = copy.deepcopy(a)

quiz.question: What does list.copy() do with nested lists?
choices: It copies only the outer list (shallow)
quiz.explanation: Verify that the copy meets your needs.

code_smells.title: Constants as Numbers
code_smells.summary: Constants are plain numbers (STATUS = 1, 2, 3) with no meaning.
code_smells.problem: Constants are plain numbers (STATUS = 1, 2, 3) with no meaning. Code must remember what each number means.
code_smells.bad_code: if status == 2: ...   # what is 2?
code_smells.good_code:
class Status(Enum):
    NEW = 1
    PAID = 2

if status is Status.PAID: ...

quiz.question: What should replace numeric status codes?
quiz.explanation: Names tell the story numbers cannot.

code_smells.title: Premature Memoization
code_smells.summary: A function result is cached 'for speed' with no evidence it is needed.
code_smells.problem: A function result is cached 'for speed' with no evidence it is needed. The cache adds complexity and stale data risk.
code_smells.bad_code:
@lru_cache
def discount(user): ...   # depends on changing state
code_smells.good_code: def discount(user): ...   # simple; add caching after measuring

quiz.question: When should you add memoization?
choices: After measuring a real performance problem
quiz.explanation: Optimise based on evidence.

code_smells.title: Collections Empty
code_smells.summary: Code checks `len(x) == 0` (or count() == 0) where a clear, intention-revealing method like `is_empty()` or `not x` would do.
code_smells.problem: Code checks `len(x) == 0` (or count() == 0) where a clear, intention-revealing method like `is_empty()` or `not x` would do.
why_bad: May be slow for some collections.
code_smells.bad_code: if len(items) == 0: ...
code_smells.good_code: if not items: ...   # or items.is_empty()
fix: Add is_empty() to your own collections.

quiz.question: Which is more Pythonic?
quiz.explanation: Say what you mean: it is empty.

code_smells.title: NullCustomer
code_smells.summary: A class is called NullCustomer or NullUser after the technical pattern, not after the real-world concept (a guest, an unknown visitor).
code_smells.problem: A class is called NullCustomer or NullUser after the technical pattern, not after the real-world concept (a guest, an unknown visitor).
code_smells.bad_code: class NullCustomer(Customer): ...
code_smells.good_code: class GuestCustomer(Customer): ...

quiz.question: Which name fits the domain better?
quiz.explanation: Use domain names, not pattern names.

code_smells.title: Silent Truncation
code_smells.summary: Text is cut to a fixed length in some places (UI) but not others (database), so data is silently truncated or rejected.
code_smells.problem: Text is cut to a fixed length in some places (UI) but not others (database), so data is silently truncated or rejected.
code_smells.bad_code: name = text[:20]   # elsewhere: 50 allowed
fix: Enforce it in the domain object.

quiz.question: Where should a maximum length be enforced?
quiz.explanation: Silent truncation loses data.

code_smells.title: Mystery Guest
code_smells.summary: A test relies on data created somewhere else (a database row, a fixture file), so a reader cannot see what the test depends on.
code_smells.problem: A test relies on data created somewhere else (a database row, a fixture file), so a reader cannot see what the test depends on.
code_smells.bad_code:
def test_total():
    assert Order.get(42).total() == 250   # who is order 42?
fix: Create the data inside the test.

quiz.question: What is a 'mystery guest' in tests?
choices: Test data defined somewhere you cannot see
quiz.explanation: Make test setup visible.

code_smells.title: Parallel Hierarchies
code_smells.summary: Two class hierarchies mirror each other (Shape and ShapeRenderer).
code_smells.problem: Two class hierarchies mirror each other (Shape and ShapeRenderer). Adding a class to one forces a new class in the other.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Circle: ...
class CircleRenderer: ...
class Square: ...
class SquareRenderer: ...
code_smells.good_code:
class Circle:
    def draw(self, canvas): ...

quiz.question: What is a parallel hierarchy problem?
choices: Adding a class in one hierarchy forces one in the other
quiz.explanation: Keep behavior with its data.

code_smells.title: Mutable Getters
code_smells.summary: A getter returns the internal list, so callers can add and remove items from outside and break the object.
code_smells.problem: A getter returns the internal list, so callers can add and remove items from outside and break the object.
code_smells.bad_code: def items(self): return self._items   # callers can append
code_smells.good_code: def items(self): return tuple(self._items)   # a copy

quiz.question: What should a getter return for an internal list?
choices: A copy or an immutable view
quiz.explanation: Protect your internals.

code_smells.title: Name With Collections
code_smells.summary: Collections are named with the word 'collection' (user_collection, order_collection).
code_smells.problem: Collections are named with the word 'collection' (user_collection, order_collection). The plural already says it.
code_smells.bad_code: user_collection, order_collection
code_smells.good_code: users, orders

quiz.question: Which name is better?
quiz.explanation: Plural nouns say it all.

code_smells.title: Secrets in Code
code_smells.summary: Passwords, API keys and tokens are written in the source code, which ends up in version control and logs.
code_smells.problem: Passwords, API keys and tokens are written in the source code, which ends up in version control and logs.
code_smells.bad_code: API_KEY = 'sk-live-123456'
code_smells.good_code: API_KEY = os.environ['API_KEY']
fix: Move secrets to environment variables or a secrets manager.

quiz.question: Where should API keys be stored?
choices: Outside the code: environment or a secrets manager
quiz.explanation: Never commit secrets.

code_smells.title: Testing with External Resources
code_smells.summary: Tests read files, call APIs or use the internet.
code_smells.problem: Tests read files, call APIs or use the internet. They fail when the resource changes or is unavailable.
code_smells.bad_code:
def test_report():
    data = open('/home/me/sales.csv').read()
code_smells.good_code:
def test_report():
    data = io.StringIO('a,b\n1,2')

quiz.question: How should a test get its input data?
quiz.explanation: Tests must control their inputs.

code_smells.title: Crowdstrike NULL
code_smells.summary: Code dereferences a null pointer in critical software.
code_smells.problem: Code dereferences a null pointer in critical software. A single missing check can crash the whole system.
code_smells.bad_code:
int *p = NULL;

code_smells.good_code: domain = 'my-site.example.com'

quiz.question: Which is a valid hostname label?
quiz.explanation: Respect the rules of the standard.

code_smells.title: Not Replaced Constants

code_smells.problem: Default or example keys and constants from documentation are never replaced, leaving production with public values.

code_smells.title: Squatting

choices: Predictable names can be guessed or taken by attackers

code_smells.title: Hanlon's Razor
code_smells.summary: Code checks for situations that cannot happen (impossible nulls, checked twice).
code_smells.problem: Code checks for situations that cannot happen (impossible nulls, checked twice). The extra checks add noise.

code_smells.title: Linguistic Confusion

code_smells.title: Collection Aliasing
code_smells.summary: Two variables point to the same list.
code_smells.problem: Two variables point to the same list. Changing one silently changes the other (aliasing).

b = a
b.append(3)   # a is [1, 2, 3] too
code_smells.good_code: b = a.copy()   # or use tuples

quiz.explanation: Assignment copies the reference, not the list.

code_smells.title: Objects Aliasing
code_smells.summary: Two names refer to the same mutable object.
code_smells.problem: Two names refer to the same mutable object. A change through one name is visible through the other.

p2 = p1

code_smells.good_code: p2 = replace(p1, name='Bala')   # frozen dataclass copy

quiz.question: How do you prevent aliasing surprises?
choices: Use immutable objects or copy them
quiz.explanation: Immutable objects cannot be changed by accident.

code_smells.title: Ternary Metaprogramming

code_smells.problem: A ternary picks which method to call by name (obj.a() if x else obj.b()), or dynamic names built from strings. It is hard to follow and refactor.

quiz.question: Why avoid `getattr(obj, name)()` with computed names?
choices: It is hard to read and tools cannot track the calls
quiz.explanation: Be explicit about which method runs.

code_smells.title: Low-Level Addition
code_smells.summary: Hand-written loops perform simple sums, filters and maps.
code_smells.problem: Hand-written loops perform simple sums, filters and maps. A declarative style says the goal in one line.

quiz.question: Which is more declarative?
choices: sum(x for x in nums if x > 0)
A manual for loop with total
quiz.explanation: Say what, not how.

code_smells.title: Boolean APIs

code_smells.problem: An API has a boolean parameter like `admin=true` to switch to a powerful mode. One flag changes security rules.

code_smells.good_code:
POST /users           # normal
POST /admin/users     # separate, protected endpoint

quiz.question: What is safer than an `admin=true` flag?
quiz.explanation: Different powers deserve different doors.

code_smells.title: The Hollywood Principle
code_smells.summary: Low-level code decides when to call high-level code, creating tight links in both directions.
code_smells.problem: Low-level code decides when to call high-level code, creating tight links in both directions. The Hollywood Principle says: 'Don't call us, we'll call you'.

class Logger:
    def log(self): app = App(); app.report()   # low level calls high level
fix: Let high-level code decide when to call.

quiz.question: What does the Hollywood Principle say?
choices: High-level code calls low-level code, not the reverse
quiz.explanation: Invert control to keep coupling loose.

code_smells.title: API Chain
code_smells.summary: A test calls an API again and again to check one result, chaining extra requests when one direct check would be enough.
code_smells.problem: A test calls an API again and again to check one result, chaining extra requests when one direct check would be enough.

code_smells.good_code:
r = client.post('/users')
assert r.json()['name'] == 'Asha'

quiz.question: Why avoid long API call chains inside a test?
choices: They make tests slow and fragile
quiz.explanation: Test the primitive result.

code_smells.title: Overengineering
code_smells.summary: A simple problem is solved with layers, patterns and options 'for flexibility'.
code_smells.problem: A simple problem is solved with layers, patterns and options 'for flexibility'. The solution is far more complex than the problem.
code_smells.bad_code: class AbstractFactoryProviderStrategy: ...   # to print 'hello'
code_smells.good_code: print('hello')

quiz.question: What does KISS stand for?
quiz.explanation: Simple solutions are easier to maintain.

code_smells.title: Cascaded Returns

code_smells.problem: A function has many return statements in nested branches, making it hard to know where it ends and what it gives back.

def f(x):

    return 2
fix: Use early returns and guard clauses.

quiz.question: What flattens nested returns?
quiz.explanation: Handle edge cases first.

code_smells.title: Missing Test Wrong Path
code_smells.summary: A test checks that a function raises an exception but does not fail if it does not raise.
code_smells.problem: A test checks that a function raises an exception but does not fail if it does not raise. The test passes even when the code is broken.

quiz.question: How do you assert that a function raises an error in pytest?
quiz.explanation: A test must be able to fail.

code_smells.title: Untested Regular Expressions
code_smells.summary: Regular expressions are added without tests.
code_smells.problem: Regular expressions are added without tests. Nobody knows what they match, and edge cases slip through.

code_smells.good_code:
assert is_email('a@b.com')
assert not is_email('a@')
assert not is_email('@b.com')
fix: Write test cases for the regex.

quiz.question: What should accompany every non-trivial regex?
choices: Tests with valid and invalid examples
quiz.explanation: Test patterns like any other code.

code_smells.title: UPPERCASE Acronyms
code_smells.summary: Acronyms are written in all capitals inside names (HTTPServerURLParser).
code_smells.problem: Acronyms are written in all capitals inside names (HTTPServerURLParser). Words run together and are hard to read.

class HttpUrlParser: ...
def parse_urls(): ...

quiz.question: Which is easiest to read?
quiz.explanation: Capitalise like normal words.

code_smells.title: DirName and File

code_smells.problem: Names mix concept and context, like dir_name and file when they hold paths, so readers must guess what they contain.

directory_path = Path('/tmp')

quiz.question: What does a variable `file` hold in `file = '/tmp/a.txt'`?
choices: A path, so it should be named path

code_smells.title: Loop Premature Optimization
code_smells.summary: Loops are rewritten with clever tricks for speed with no measurement.
code_smells.problem: Loops are rewritten with clever tricks for speed with no measurement. The code gets harder to read without being faster where it counts.

i = 0; n = len(x)
while i < n: ...   # 'faster' than for
code_smells.good_code: for item in x: ...

quiz.question: When should you optimise a loop?
choices: When profiling shows it is a bottleneck
quiz.explanation: Clarity first, speed from evidence.

code_smells.title: Spaghetti Code
code_smells.summary: Control jumps around with GOTO-like statements, so you cannot follow the program from top to bottom.
code_smells.problem: Control jumps around with GOTO-like statements, so you cannot follow the program from top to bottom.

10 IF x > 5 THEN GOTO 40
20 PRINT 'small'
30 GOTO 50
40 PRINT 'big'
code_smells.good_code: print('big' if x > 5 else 'small')
fix: Use structured code: loops and functions.

quiz.question: What replaces GOTO in structured code?
quiz.explanation: Structured code reads top to bottom.

code_smells.title: Hashes
code_smells.summary: Two objects that are equal must have the same hash.
code_smells.problem: Two objects that are equal must have the same hash. If __eq__ and __hash__ disagree, dictionaries and sets lose items or hold duplicates.

quiz.question: What must be true for two equal objects?
choices: They must have the same hash
quiz.explanation: The equals/hash contract keeps collections working.

code_smells.title: Bad Defaults
code_smells.summary: Code treats an unknown response or unexpected value as 'OK' by default.
code_smells.problem: Code treats an unknown response or unexpected value as 'OK' by default. An attacker or error is then accepted.

code_smells.good_code:
if response.get('status') != 'ok':
    raise Unauthorized()

quiz.question: What should the default be for an unknown permission result?
quiz.explanation: Secure by default.

code_smells.title: Unresolved Meta Tags
code_smells.summary: Templates leave placeholders like {name} or null in output (emails, pages) because a value was missing.
code_smells.problem: Templates leave placeholders like {name} or null in output (emails, pages) because a value was missing.
code_smells.bad_code: f'Hi {user.name}!'   # prints 'Hi None!'
code_smells.good_code:
if not user.name: raise ValueError('name required')
f'Hi {user.name}!'

quiz.question: What can happen with a missing template value?
choices: 'None' or a raw {placeholder} appears in the output
quiz.explanation: Validate before you render.

code_smells.title: Encrypted Functions
code_smells.summary: Code is obfuscated (minified or encrypted logic, cryptic names) so nobody can review what it really does.
code_smells.problem: Code is obfuscated (minified or encrypted logic, cryptic names) so nobody can review what it really does.
code_smells.bad_code: def a(b,c): return (b^c)&0xFF   # ???
code_smells.good_code: def checksum(data, key): return (data ^ key) & 0xFF

quiz.question: Why is obfuscated shared code a problem?
choices: Nobody can review or trust it
quiz.explanation: Code should be readable by humans.

code_smells.title: Non-Imperative Functions Names
code_smells.summary: Function names are nouns or vague (data, handler, thing) instead of actions (calculate_total).
code_smells.problem: Function names are nouns or vague (data, handler, thing) instead of actions (calculate_total). Readers cannot tell what they do.
code_smells.bad_code: def user_data(): ...
code_smells.good_code: def load_user(): ...

quiz.question: Which function name is best?
quiz.explanation: Functions do things; name them with verbs.

code_smells.title: Overlapping Methods

code_smells.problem: A child class defines a method with the same name as a parent's private helper. The child's method accidentally replaces it.

class A:

quiz.question: How can a child accidentally break a parent's private method?
choices: By defining a method with the same name
quiz.explanation: Private names should not collide.

code_smells.title: Unused Local Assignment
code_smells.summary: A variable is assigned a value that is never read.
code_smells.problem: A variable is assigned a value that is never read. The line suggests importance but does nothing.

code_smells.good_code: compute()   # or remove if it has no effect

quiz.question: What should you do with an assignment whose value is never used?
quiz.explanation: Only keep lines that matter.

code_smells.title: Unthrown Exceptions
code_smells.summary: An exception object is created but never raised (`ValueError('bad')` without raise).
code_smells.problem: An exception object is created but never raised (`ValueError('bad')` without raise). The error is silently ignored.
code_smells.bad_code:
if x < 0:
    ValueError('negative')   # forgot raise
code_smells.good_code:
if x < 0:
    raise ValueError('negative')

quiz.question: What does `ValueError('x')` do on its own?
choices: Nothing; it only creates an object
quiz.explanation: Remember the raise keyword.

code_smells.title: Shy Visitor

code_smells.problem: The Visitor pattern is combined with isinstance checks inside the visitor, defeating the purpose of double dispatch.

choices: The visitor should dispatch by type, not by ifs

code_smells.title: Refused Bequest
code_smells.summary: A subclass inherits methods it does not want, then overrides them with nothing or errors.
code_smells.problem: A subclass inherits methods it does not want, then overrides them with nothing or errors. The hierarchy is wrong.

class Penguin(Bird):

code_smells.good_code:
class Bird: ...
class FlyingBird(Bird):
    def fly(self): ...

quiz.question: A subclass refuses to implement an inherited method. What is the problem?
quiz.explanation: Children must honour the parent's contract.

code_smells.title: Mutable Keys
code_smells.summary: Objects used as dictionary keys are later changed.

class Point: x: int; y: int
fix: Do not change keys after use.

quiz.question: What makes a safe dictionary key?
quiz.explanation: Keys must not change.

code_smells.title: Missing Return

code_smells.problem: A function forgets to return on some path, so it returns None unexpectedly and callers break.

def grade(s):
    if s > 90: return 'A'
    elif s > 80: return 'B'

code_smells.good_code:
def grade(s):
    if s > 90: return 'A'
    if s > 80: return 'B'
    return 'C'

quiz.question: What does a Python function return when it ends without `return`?
quiz.explanation: Make every path return a value.

code_smells.title: isTesting
code_smells.summary: Code has an `is_testing` flag so it can behave differently under test.
code_smells.problem: Code has an `is_testing` flag so it can behave differently under test. Tests then do not exercise the real behavior.

class Service:

quiz.question: How do you replace behavior in tests without flags?
quiz.explanation: Tests should not change production code paths.

code_smells.title: Implicit Return
code_smells.summary: Behavior depends on implicit returns (the last expression is returned) so readers must work out what comes back.
code_smells.problem: Behavior depends on implicit returns (the last expression is returned) so readers must work out what comes back.

quiz.question: Why can implicit returns hurt readability?
choices: The returned value is hard to spot
quiz.explanation: Explicit is better than implicit.

code_smells.title: String Concatenation
code_smells.summary: Messages are built by joining many strings and variables with +.
code_smells.problem: Messages are built by joining many strings and variables with +. The text is hard to read and easy to break.

code_smells.good_code: msg = f'Hello {name}, you have {n} new messages.'

quiz.explanation: Templates read like the final text.

code_smells.title: Unhappy to the Right

if not ok: raise Invalid
if not allowed: raise Denied
do()
fix: Keep the main flow at the left.

choices: At the end of the file
Along the left margin, after the guard clauses
quiz.explanation: Guard clauses keep code flat.

code_smells.title: Syntactic Noise
code_smells.summary: Code is packed with symbols (`?:`, `&&`, `!!`, regex-like one-liners) that only experts can decode.
code_smells.problem: Code is packed with symbols (`?:`, `&&`, `!!`, regex-like one-liners) that only experts can decode.

quiz.question: What reduces syntactic noise?
choices: Naming intermediate values and splitting expressions
quiz.explanation: Make code read like prose.

code_smells.title: Microsoft Windows Time Waste

code_smells.problem: Initialization code skips reporting that it is finished on some paths, so other parts wait or time out.

quiz.explanation: Every path must report success or failure.

code_smells.title: Overloaded Test Setup

code_smells.title: Database as Parameter

quiz.explanation: Status codes are part of the API contract.

code_smells.title: Null Pointer Exception

code_smells.title: AI External Comments
