code_smells.title: Vague Date Naming
code_smells.summary: Variables are called `date` or `time`, so readers cannot tell which date it is (created, due, birth).
code_smells.problem: Variables are called `date` or `time`, so readers cannot tell which date it is (created, due, birth). The name only describes the type.
code_smells.bad_code: date = order.date
code_smells.good_code:
ordered_on = order.ordered_on
delivery_due = order.delivery_due
fix: Name the role of the date.

quiz.question: Which name is clearest?
quiz.explanation: A date has a business meaning; name it.

code_smells.title: Plain Text Passwords
code_smells.summary: Passwords are stored or compared as plain text.
code_smells.problem: Passwords are stored or compared as plain text. If the data leaks, every account is exposed.
code_smells.bad_code: if user.password == entered: login()
code_smells.good_code: if bcrypt.checkpw(entered.encode(), user.password_hash): login()
fix: Hash passwords with a strong algorithm.

quiz.question: How should passwords be stored?
quiz.explanation: Never keep recoverable passwords.

code_smells.title: Too Many Asserts
code_smells.summary: One test contains many assertions about different things.
code_smells.problem: One test contains many assertions about different things. When it fails, you must dig to know which one broke.
code_smells.bad_code:
def test_user():
    assert u.name == 'A'; assert u.age == 3; assert u.email; assert u.active
code_smells.good_code:
def test_name(): assert u.name == 'A'
def test_age(): assert u.age == 3

quiz.question: Why prefer one assertion per test?
choices: A failure points to exactly one problem
quiz.explanation: Focused tests give clear failures.

code_smells.title: Workslop Code
code_smells.summary: AI-generated code is accepted because it looks plausible, but nobody checks if it does the right thing.
code_smells.problem: AI-generated code is accepted because it looks plausible, but nobody checks if it does the right thing. It has hollow logic and misses edge cases.
code_smells.bad_code: def total(items): return sum(items) if items else 0   # for prices as strings?
code_smells.good_code: def total(items: list[Decimal]) -> Decimal: ...   # reviewed and tested

quiz.question: What should you do with AI-generated code?
choices: Review and test it before accepting
quiz.explanation: AI output still needs review.

code_smells.title: Model Collapse
code_smells.summary: Repeated AI edits slowly change names and structure until the original domain terms are lost and logic is duplicated.
code_smells.problem: Repeated AI edits slowly change names and structure until the original domain terms are lost and logic is duplicated.
code_smells.bad_code: # Customer -> Client -> User -> Account after four AI edits
code_smells.good_code: # keep one domain term; golden tests protect behavior

quiz.question: What protects code from drift after many AI edits?
quiz.explanation: Do not let tools erode your model.

code_smells.title: Cloudflare Feature Explosion
code_smells.summary: A huge auto-generated config file is loaded without limits or validation.
code_smells.problem: A huge auto-generated config file is loaded without limits or validation. Growing too big crashes the system.
code_smells.bad_code: features = load(config)   # assumes < 200 entries
code_smells.good_code: if len(features) > MAX_FEATURES: raise ConfigTooLarge()

quiz.question: What should code do with an unexpectedly huge config?
quiz.explanation: Check generated input before using it.

code_smells.title: Nitpicking
code_smells.summary: Code reviews focus on small style points (spacing, naming) and miss design, security and intent problems.
code_smells.problem: Code reviews focus on small style points (spacing, naming) and miss design, security and intent problems.
code_smells.bad_code: # review comments: 'add a space', 'rename x' ... on a PR with a SQL injection
code_smells.good_code: # automate style; reviewers focus on design, security and tests

quiz.question: What should human reviewers focus on?
quiz.explanation: Let tools do the nitpicking.

code_smells.title: Email Handling Vulnerabilities
code_smells.summary: A system looks up users by a normalised email, but sends mail to whatever the UI supplied.
code_smells.problem: A system looks up users by a normalised email, but sends mail to whatever the UI supplied. Identity and delivery can differ.
code_smells.bad_code:
user = find(email.lower())
send(ui_email)   # may be different
code_smells.good_code:
email = canonical(ui_email)
user = find(email)
send(email)
fix: Let the server own the canonical value.

quiz.question: Where should the canonical email be decided?
quiz.explanation: One identity, one canonical form.

code_smells.title: Refactoring Dirty Code
code_smells.summary: Time is spent refactoring code that never changes while the files that change every week stay messy.
code_smells.problem: Time is spent refactoring code that never changes while the files that change every week stay messy.
code_smells.bad_code: # refactor a 5-year-old stable module nobody touches
code_smells.good_code: # git log shows the 5 files changed most; refactor those first
fix: Check change frequency in version control.

quiz.question: Which code should you refactor first?
choices: Code that changes often and is hard to read
quiz.explanation: Spend effort where it pays off.

code_smells.title: Hardcoded Stateless Properties
code_smells.summary: A class creates its own helper (`self.calc = TaxCalculator()`) in the constructor.
code_smells.problem: A class creates its own helper (`self.calc = TaxCalculator()`) in the constructor. It is hardwired and cannot be swapped or tested alone.
code_smells.bad_code:
class Shop:
    def __init__(self): self.calc = TaxCalculator()
code_smells.good_code:
class Shop:
    def __init__(self, calc): self.calc = calc
fix: Or use a function if it has no state.

quiz.question: How do you make `Shop` independent of a specific TaxCalculator?
quiz.explanation: Dependency injection loosens coupling.

code_smells.title: Vanity Coverage
code_smells.summary: Tests that execute code to raise coverage but assert nothing meaningful.
code_smells.problem: The coverage number looks great because every line runs, yet the tests would still pass if the code were wrong.
why_bad: Coverage becomes a target instead of a measure.
code_smells.bad_code:
def test_total():
    cart.total()   # runs the code, asserts nothing
code_smells.good_code:
def test_total():
    assert cart.total() == 250
fix: Try mutation testing to find tests that never fail.

quiz.question: A test calls a function but never asserts. What is it good for?
quiz.explanation: Coverage measures what ran, not what was checked.

code_smells.title: Getter Piggybacking
code_smells.summary: Reusing a display getter from outside to bolt on business rules.
code_smells.problem: A getter exists to show a value. Other functions reuse it and add their own comparisons, so the same rule is duplicated outside the object.
fix: Add behavior methods to the object.

quiz.question: Two functions each compare food.use_by_date to today. What is the best fix?
choices: Copy the comparison into a helper module
quiz.explanation: Let the object answer the question so the rule exists once, in the owner.

code_smells.title: Long Functions
code_smells.summary: One function doing many things at several levels of detail.
code_smells.problem: A function grows to dozens of lines handling validation, calculation, persistence and formatting together.
why_bad: Changes in one area risk another.
code_smells.good_code:
def checkout(cart):
    validate(cart)
    total = apply_discounts(cart)
    charge(total)
    send_receipt(cart)
fix: Extract cohesive blocks into well-named functions.
Make the top-level function read like an outline.

quiz.question: Which refactoring best fixes a 100-line function?
quiz.explanation: Extract Function turns each step into a named, testable unit; the original reads as a summary.

code_smells.title: Primitive Obsession
code_smells.summary: Using raw strings and numbers for domain concepts like emails, money or ids.
code_smells.problem: Concepts with rules are passed around as plain str/int/float, so validation and behavior are repeated everywhere.
why_bad: Invalid values travel far before failing.
Mixing up arguments of the same type is easy.
code_smells.bad_code:
def send(to: str, amount: float): ...
send('not-an-email', -5)
fix: Create small value objects for domain concepts.

quiz.question: What does wrapping an email string in an Email value object give you?
choices: A single place that guarantees it is valid
quiz.explanation: A value object validates on creation, so every Email you hold is already known to be valid.

code_smells.title: Mutable Default Argument
code_smells.summary: A list or dict as default value is shared between calls.
code_smells.problem: Python evaluates default values once, at definition time, so a mutable default accumulates changes across calls.
why_bad: Bugs that appear only on later calls.
code_smells.bad_code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1); add(2)  # [1, 2] on second call
fix: Default to None and create the object inside.

quiz.question: What does add(1) then add(2) return for the second call with def add(item, bucket=[])?
quiz.explanation: The default list is created once and reused, so it keeps the earlier item.

code_smells.title: Swallowed Exceptions
code_smells.summary: A bare except that hides failures.
code_smells.problem: Catching everything and ignoring it makes errors vanish. The program continues in a broken state.
why_bad: Also catches KeyboardInterrupt with a bare except.
fix: Log or re-raise; never silently pass.

quiz.question: What is wrong with `except: pass`?
choices: It hides errors, including ones you did not expect
quiz.explanation: Silent failure turns a clear crash into a mysterious wrong result.

code_smells.title: Boolean Flag Parameters
code_smells.summary: A True/False argument that switches a function between two behaviors.
code_smells.problem: Calls like render(page, True) are unreadable, and the function secretly does two jobs.
code_smells.good_code:
def send_urgent(msg): ...
def send_normal(msg): ...
fix: Or use keyword-only arguments / an enum.

quiz.question: Why is send(msg, True) a smell?
choices: The reader cannot tell what True means
quiz.explanation: Flags hide intent and signal that the function has more than one responsibility.

code_smells.title: Long Parameter List
code_smells.summary: Functions that take many arguments.
code_smells.problem: Five or more parameters are hard to remember, easy to pass in the wrong order and often belong together.
code_smells.bad_code: def create_user(name, email, street, city, zip, country, phone, plan): ...
fix: Group related args into an object.

quiz.question: Street, city, zip and country keep travelling together. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: Data that travels together deserves a name and a home.

code_smells.title: Duplicated Code
code_smells.summary: The same logic copied in several places.
code_smells.problem: Copy-paste speeds today and slows every future change, since each copy must be fixed.
why_bad: Bugs are fixed in one place and missed in another.
More code to read and maintain.
code_smells.bad_code:
tax_a = price * 0.18
...
tax_b = cost * 0.18
code_smells.good_code:
def gst(amount):
    return amount * GST_RATE
fix: Name it for the idea, not the use.

quiz.question: What risk does duplicated code create?
choices: A fix applied in one copy but not the others
quiz.explanation: Copies drift apart; one shared function keeps behavior consistent.

code_smells.title: Global State and Singletons
code_smells.summary: Hidden shared state that any code can change.
code_smells.problem: Modules read and write global variables or singletons, so behavior depends on invisible state.
code_smells.good_code:
def greet(user):
    return f'Hi {user.name}'
fix: Limit mutable state to small scopes.

quiz.question: Why do globals make tests harder?
choices: Tests share and depend on hidden state
quiz.explanation: A test cannot control state it cannot see, and leaked state couples tests together.

code_smells.title: Comments That Say 'What'
code_smells.summary: Comments that repeat the code instead of explaining why.
code_smells.problem: When a comment narrates the code, it duplicates it, goes stale and signals names are unclear.
code_smells.bad_code:
# increment i by one
i += 1

# check if user is adult
if u.a >= 18:
code_smells.good_code: if user.is_adult():
fix: Rename to make the code self-explanatory.
Keep comments for why, not what.

quiz.question: Which comment is worth keeping?
choices: # Retry: the payment API is eventually consistent after refunds
quiz.explanation: Good comments capture reasons the code cannot express.

code_smells.title: Deep Nesting (Arrow Code)
code_smells.summary: Layers of nested if statements pushing code to the right.
code_smells.problem: Each nested condition adds a level to remember. The happy path gets buried.
code_smells.good_code:
def pay(order):
    if not order: return
    if not order.valid: return
    if not order.user.active: return
    charge(order)
fix: Use guard clauses and return early.

quiz.question: What technique flattens deeply nested conditionals?
quiz.explanation: Handle the exceptional cases first and leave the main path unindented.

code_smells.title: God Class
code_smells.summary: One class that knows and does too much.
code_smells.problem: A class collects unrelated responsibilities until everything depends on it and nobody dares to edit it.
code_smells.bad_code:
class App:
    def login(self): ...
    def charge_card(self): ...
    def render_pdf(self): ...
    def send_email(self): ...
code_smells.good_code:
class Auth: ...
class Payments: ...
class Reports: ...
class Mailer: ...
fix: Move behavior to the objects that own the data.

quiz.question: Which principle does a God Class violate most directly?
quiz.explanation: A class should have one reason to change.

code_smells.title: Dead Code
code_smells.summary: Code that is never executed but still has to be read.
code_smells.problem: Old branches, unused functions and commented-out blocks stay behind 'just in case'.
why_bad: Looks important so people maintain it.
code_smells.good_code: # deleted — git history keeps it
fix: Use coverage and linters to find unused code.

quiz.question: Why is it safe to delete commented-out code?
quiz.explanation: Git remembers, so the working tree can stay clean.

code_smells.title: Misleading and Abbreviated Names
code_smells.summary: Names like d, tmp, data or mgr that hide meaning.
code_smells.problem: Readers must decode abbreviations and generic names, and names that lie are worse than none.
code_smells.good_code:
def total_price(unit_price, quantity):
    return unit_price * quantity

quiz.question: Which name is best for a list of overdue invoices?
quiz.explanation: A good name tells the reader what and why without a comment.

code_smells.title: If/Elif Chains on Type
code_smells.summary: Branching on a kind or type code everywhere.
code_smells.problem: The same if/elif ladder appears in many places; adding a new kind means editing all of them.
code_smells.bad_code:
if shape.kind == 'circle': area = 3.14 * r * r
elif shape.kind == 'square': area = s * s
fix: Let each type own its behavior.

quiz.question: What does polymorphism replace in this smell?
quiz.explanation: Each class implements the same method, so callers just call it.

code_smells.title: Speculative Generality
code_smells.summary: Abstractions built for needs that never arrive.
code_smells.problem: Extra layers, hooks and parameters 'in case we need them' add complexity with no current benefit.
code_smells.bad_code: class AbstractPluginFactoryManager: ...   # one plugin exists
code_smells.good_code: def load_plugin(name): ...
fix: Generalise when the second case appears.

quiz.question: What does YAGNI stand for?
quiz.explanation: Don't add what you don't need yet.

code_smells.title: Shotgun Surgery
code_smells.summary: One small change forces edits in many files.
code_smells.problem: A single concept is scattered, so changing it means touching a dozen places.
code_smells.bad_code: # changing the date format means editing 12 modules
code_smells.good_code: # one format_date() used everywhere
fix: Gather the scattered logic into one place.

quiz.question: A tiny change needs edits in many files. What is the cause?
choices: A concept's logic is spread out instead of centralised
quiz.explanation: Cohesion: things that change together should live together.

code_smells.title: Data Clumps
code_smells.summary: The same group of values always passed around together.
code_smells.problem: start_date, end_date or lat, lng appear side by side across many signatures.
code_smells.bad_code:
def book(start, end, ...): ...
def cancel(start, end, ...): ...
fix: Create a small object for the group.

quiz.question: If three values always travel together, what is likely missing?
quiz.explanation: A named concept removes repetition and attracts related behavior.

code_smells.title: Hardcoded Configuration and Secrets
code_smells.summary: Passwords, keys and URLs written in source code.
code_smells.problem: Credentials committed to a repository leak and make every environment share the same values.
code_smells.bad_code:
API_KEY = 'sk-live-123456'
DB = 'postgres://admin:pw@prod/db'
code_smells.good_code:
import os
API_KEY = os.environ['API_KEY']
fix: Read from environment variables or a secret manager.

quiz.question: Where should an API key live?
quiz.explanation: Keep secrets out of version control so they can differ per environment and stay private.

code_smells.title: Mutating Arguments
code_smells.summary: Functions that silently modify the objects passed in.
code_smells.problem: The caller's data changes behind its back, so results depend on call order.
why_bad: Hard to reason about and test.
code_smells.good_code:
def with_tax(items):
    return [{**i, 'price': i['price'] * 1.18} for i in items]
fix: Document it if mutation is intended.

quiz.question: What is the risk of mutating a list passed as an argument?
quiz.explanation: Hidden side effects make code unpredictable; prefer returning new values.

code_smells.title: Premature Optimization
code_smells.summary: Making code harder to read for speed nobody measured.
code_smells.problem: Complex tricks are added before knowing where the time actually goes.
code_smells.bad_code: # hand-rolled cache and bit tricks in a function called twice a day
code_smells.good_code: # write it clearly, profile, then optimise the hot spot

quiz.question: What should come before optimising?
quiz.explanation: Make it work, make it clear, then make it fast where measurements say it matters.

code_smells.title: Hidden Time Dependency
code_smells.summary: Calling datetime.now() deep inside logic, making tests flaky.
code_smells.problem: Hidden clock access means results change with the moment you run, so tests can't control time.
code_smells.bad_code:
def is_expired(item):
    return item.expires < datetime.now()
code_smells.good_code:
def is_expired(item, now):
    return item.expires < now
fix: Pass the time (or a clock) in.
Inject dependencies instead of fetching them.

quiz.question: How do you make time-dependent code testable?
choices: Pass the current time in as an argument
quiz.explanation: Injecting the clock lets a test choose any moment.
